passage:
“Did you hear what Meghna did in the client call?” Vaibhav leaned over the lunch table, grinning, to Jaya and two others.
“I heard she stayed till nine to fix the deck,” Jaya said, and opened her tiffin.
“No, but before that—”
“I'd rather hear it from Meghna.” Jaya passed the pickle. “Rohan, your part of the report is due at four. Still on track?”
“Nearly. Thanks for reminding me.”
“And Vaibhav, the slide with the supplier numbers was yours. I'll say so in the review.”
Vaibhav shrugged, quiet for a moment. Later, when the manager asked who could handle the difficult client, Rohan said, “Jaya. She does what she says.” Two others nodded.

qa.q: What did Jaya say she would do about the supplier-numbers slide?
qa.a: Jaya said she would say in the review that the slide with the supplier numbers was Vaibhav's.

qa.q: Why did Jaya answer, “I'd rather hear it from Meghna”?
qa.a: Jaya seems to avoid gossip and to want to respect Meghna, so she turns the talk to something fair and practical. 🙂

qa.q: What made the team trust Jaya with the difficult client?
qa.a: Jaya keeps commitments, credits others and stays out of gossip, so Rohan could say, “She does what she says,” and others agreed.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav have felt when Jaya credited Vaibhav for the slide?
qa.a: Vaibhav may have felt surprised, caught between the gossip Vaibhav started and the credit received, which fits the shrug and a quiet moment.

grounding: A person keeps commitments, credits others and avoids gossip, and gains quiet influence.

passage: I'm Binita, and when I joined the firm I watched two ways of getting ahead. Divyansh worked the corridors: favours, flattery, a quiet word against whoever stood in his way. I kept my promises, even the small ones, like sending the minutes the same evening. I put people's names on their work in every deck and left the gossip alone. For a year it seemed slow. Divyansh was invited to more lunches. Then the company restructured, and the partners asked around about who could be trusted with the big account. Several people said my name, and one said, “When Binita says Thursday, it's Thursday.” Divyansh's favours had mostly dried up. Looking back, I never felt clever. I just felt steady.

qa.q: What small promise did Binita keep every time?
qa.a: Binita sent the minutes the same evening.

qa.q: How did Binita feel during the first year when Divyansh was invited to more lunches?
qa.a: Binita probably felt overlooked and a little doubtful while Divyansh got the lunches, yet kept a quiet patience.

qa.q: What choice did Binita keep making during the slow first year, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Binita kept small promises, credited others and stayed out of gossip, and that reliability showed when the company restructured and people said, “When Binita says Thursday, it's Thursday.”

qa.q: How might Divyansh have felt when the partners asked around and his favours had mostly dried up?
qa.a: Divyansh may have felt surprised and uneasy, since the corridor alliances he built did not help when people were asked who could be trusted.

grounding: A person who keeps commitments, credits others and avoids gossip gains quiet influence that outlasts favours built on manoeuvring.

passage: Supervisor's note for the annual review, clinic front desk. When I asked the six desk staff who they go to when something goes wrong, four of them named Ojas. Ojas has been here only eighteen months. What I have seen: when Ojas says a report will be ready by Friday, it is ready by Thursday evening. When the new booking system started working, Ojas told the manager that Chandrika had found the fix. At lunch, when talk turns to who is dating whom or who will be fired, Ojas usually changes the subject or goes for a walk. Others on the desk have tried to get ahead by doing favours for the manager; that works for a while and then stops. Recommendation: make Ojas a shift lead, and ask Chandrika to co-lead the rollout of the new system.

qa.q: How many of the six desk staff named Ojas?
qa.a: Four of them.

qa.q: What might Chandrika feel on hearing that Ojas credited Chandrika for the fix?
qa.a: Chandrika likely felt valued and grateful, and trusted Ojas more.

qa.q: What is the supervisor's recommendation, and why?
qa.a: Make Ojas a shift lead and have Chandrika co-lead the rollout, because Ojas's reliability and fairness have already earned the team's trust.

qa.q: How might the staff who did favours for the manager see Ojas's rise?
qa.a: They may feel surprised or resentful, since their favours worked only for a while, while Ojas's steady reliability kept building trust.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows a colleague gaining quiet influence by keeping commitments, crediting others and avoiding gossip.

passage:
Diary, Sunday.
Two years at the bank branch today. Funny thing happened on Friday. The branch manager asked who should train the three new joiners, and the whole counter said 'Rekha' at once. Even Mahima, who usually wins everything by being the manager's favourite.
I've never brought the manager samosas. I've never told him who comes in late. I just do what I say I'll do, and when someone else solves a problem I say their name in the meeting. When the gossip starts at lunch, I eat faster.
Mahima got the last two plum assignments by flattering him. But on Friday I noticed people stopped asking her for help months ago.
I don't feel powerful. I feel steady. That's enough.
Rekha

qa.q: What did the whole counter say when asked who should train the new joiners?
qa.a: 'Rekha', all at once.

qa.q: How does Rekha feel about this reputation?
qa.a: Rekha feels steady and content rather than powerful, and finds that enough.

qa.q: Which of Rekha's habits built quiet influence?
qa.a: Doing what Rekha promises, naming others when they solve problems, and staying out of lunchtime gossip.

qa.q: How might Mahima see Friday's moment?
qa.a: Mahima, used to winning through flattery, may feel surprised or uneasy that the whole counter chose Rekha, even saying the name herself.

grounding: A reliable colleague who keeps commitments, credits others and avoids gossip gains quiet influence over a flatterer.

passage: In the block agriculture office at Sehore, favours moved like small coins. Pankaj was a master of them: a leave form signed early here, the jeep lent there, every kindness remembered and quietly collected. Ritu did something duller. If she said the soil reports would reach the villages by Friday, they reached by Friday. When the pest survey went well, she read out the names of the two field assistants who had walked the fields. When canteen talk turned to the new officer's family, she finished her tea and left. So when the district team asked who should lead the new seed trial, the room went quiet, and then the head clerk said, "Ritu. Her dates are real." Pankaj laughed, a little tightly. "I've done more people more favours." "Yes," said the clerk. "That's why they owe you. They trust her."

qa.q: By when did Ritu say the soil reports would reach the villages?
qa.a: By Friday, and they reached by Friday.

qa.q: What might Pankaj have felt when the head clerk chose Ritu?
qa.a: He was probably stung and a little jealous; the tight laugh suggests he expected his favours to count for more.

qa.q: Which of Ritu's habits built her influence, and why?
qa.a: Keeping her dates, naming the field assistants who did the work, and leaving gossip behind made people trust her without owing her anything.

qa.q: How might the two field assistants see Ritu after the pest survey?
qa.a: They likely feel valued and loyal, because she gave them credit in front of everyone instead of keeping it.

grounding: Shows a colleague whose reliability, credit to others and distance from gossip earn quiet influence that outlasts favours.
